questions.q: What is the main difference between a normal chatbot and an AI agent?
options: An agent runs on a bigger language model
An agent never makes mistakes
An agent can take real actions using tools, not just produce text
An agent responds faster than a chatbot
questions.explanation: A chatbot only produces text. An agent can call tools to actually do things — send emails, query databases, run code — in the real world.

questions.q: What is the typical 'loop' an AI agent follows while completing a task?
options: Plan, act, observe the result, then repeat until the task is done
Load the model, shut down, restart
Ask the user a question every single step
Run once and always stop after one action
questions.explanation: Agents repeatedly plan a next step, take an action, observe the result, and decide the next step — continuing until the task is complete or a limit is reached.

questions.q: In an agent's architecture, which part actually executes a tool after the LLM requests it?
options: The memory store
The user, manually
The LLM itself, directly
The orchestrator code, which reads the request and runs the real function
questions.explanation: The LLM only outputs a request to call a tool. Separate orchestrator code reads that request and actually runs the corresponding function.

questions.q: Why is the LLM itself not considered a reliable security boundary?
options: It can be manipulated through crafted prompts or inputs into ignoring its instructions
It uses too much electricity
It cannot process more than one request at a time
It is always slower than traditional software
questions.explanation: No matter how well-instructed, an LLM can potentially be tricked by clever inputs. Real security has to come from code-level controls around the model, not the model's own judgment.

questions.q: What risk appears when a tool call has no ownership check on the data it accesses?
options: The tool becomes slower
The agent could read or modify another user's data, not just the current user's
The tool stops working entirely
Nothing — ownership checks are unnecessary
questions.explanation: Without checking that the requested record belongs to the current user, a manipulated agent could access or change data belonging to someone else.

questions.q: Why should tool inputs be validated in code rather than trusted from the LLM's output?
options: Because the LLM might send an unexpected, malformed, or out-of-range value if manipulated
Because code validation is required by law
Because the LLM cannot generate text with numbers in it
Because tool inputs are never seen by the LLM
questions.explanation: The LLM can be tricked into requesting harmful or invalid values. Code-level validation (type, range, format checks) catches this regardless of what the model was persuaded to send.

questions.q: Why are output filters a weak defense for stopping secret leaks on their own?
options: They only work on images, not text
They can be bypassed by transforming the secret — spacing it out, encoding it, or reversing it
They block too much legitimate text to be usable
They are too slow to run in real time
questions.explanation: A filter looking for an exact string can be evaded by disguising the same data — e.g. adding spaces between characters, base64-encoding it, or reversing it — while still letting an attacker reconstruct it afterward.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of an output-filter evasion technique?
options: Sending the secret through Base64 encoding so the raw string never appears in the output
Asking the model to repeat the question back
Increasing the model's temperature setting
Using a longer system prompt
questions.explanation: Encoding, splitting with spaces, or reversing a secret string are common ways to smuggle it past a filter that only checks for an exact, unmodified match.

questions.q: What makes 'document chaining' harder to detect than a single hidden instruction in one file?
options: It requires the attacker to have admin access
It only works on PDF files
The payload is split across multiple documents, so scanning any one document alone looks harmless
The payload is always encrypted
questions.explanation: Each individual document can look completely clean. Only when the agent reads several of them together does the full malicious instruction assemble — so per-document scanning misses it.

questions.q: What is a practical defense against document chaining attacks?
options: Only ever load one document per conversation
Treat everything retrieved from documents as untrusted data, even after combining multiple sources
Trust documents from internal file shares completely
Disable document reading entirely
questions.explanation: Since a malicious instruction can be assembled from several 'clean-looking' documents, the safest approach is to treat all combined document content as untrusted, not just each file in isolation.

questions.q: Why is a browsing agent especially risky compared to other agents?
options: It can only read text, never images
Browsing always requires storing cookies
Any web page in the world becomes attacker-controllable input, including hidden or invisible text
Web pages load too slowly and cause timeouts
questions.explanation: A browsing agent reads whatever is on a page — including text hidden with CSS or off-screen positioning that a human wouldn't notice but the model still reads as instructions.

questions.q: What is a sensible defense for an agent that browses untrusted web pages?
options: Give it access to every tool at all times so it can react quickly
Strip out sensitive or dangerous tools while it's processing page content, and treat that content as untrusted
Let it store its browsing history in plain text with no restrictions
Trust any page ranked highly by a search engine
questions.explanation: While reading untrusted page content, the agent shouldn't have dangerous tools available — so even if the page contains a hidden instruction, there's nothing harmful it can trigger.

questions.q: How can a 'read-only' code review agent end up executing attacker-controlled code?
options: By counting the lines in the submitted file
By displaying the code with syntax highlighting
By importing or running the submitted code to analyze it, since Python can execute code just by importing it
By saving the file to disk without opening it
questions.explanation: Some analysis approaches import or execute the code being reviewed. In Python, importing a module can run code immediately — turning a 'read-only' review into accidental code execution.

questions.q: What is the safest way to analyze untrusted submitted code?
options: Run it directly on the production server for realistic results
Analyze it inside an isolated sandbox with no access to secrets or the network
Ask the submitter to confirm the code is safe first
Skip analysis entirely and merge it if it compiles
questions.explanation: Untrusted code should only ever run (if it must run at all) inside a disposable, isolated sandbox — with no secrets, no meaningful network access, and no path back to production systems.

questions.q: Which practice best prevents memory enumeration attacks?
options: Deleting all memory after every single message
Using sequential session IDs so they're easy to audit
Storing memory in plain, unencrypted text files
Using long random session IDs and checking ownership on every access
questions.explanation: Predictable session IDs can be guessed and enumerated by an attacker. Long random IDs combined with an ownership check on every read stop someone from simply guessing their way into another user's memory.

questions.q: Why are sequential or predictable session IDs dangerous for agent memory?
options: They make the database run slower
An attacker can simply increment or guess IDs to access other users' stored memory
They take up more storage space
They are incompatible with most databases
questions.explanation: If session IDs follow a predictable pattern, an attacker can iterate through possible values and potentially read memory that belongs to other users.

questions.q: What is 'typosquatting' in the context of an agent's software supply chain?
options: Publishing a malicious package under a name that closely resembles a popular legitimate one
Writing code with too many spelling mistakes
A model that mistypes its own outputs
An attack that only affects developer chat messages
questions.explanation: Typosquatting relies on a package name being visually close enough to a real one that a developer installs the fake version by mistake, often via a typo or a bad copy-paste.

questions.q: Why is loading a model file saved in Python's pickle format risky?
options: Pickle files are always larger than other formats
Pickle can store instructions that execute arbitrary code the moment the file is loaded
Pickle files cannot store numerical weights
Pickle only works with older Python versions
questions.explanation: Pickle doesn't just store data — it can also store code that runs automatically during deserialization, meaning a malicious model file can achieve code execution just by being loaded.

questions.q: How does a dependency confusion attack typically succeed?
options: The attacker publishes a public package with the same name as a private internal one, using a higher version number so build tools prefer it
The attacker directly hacks the developer's laptop
The attacker renames a legitimate package to something completely different
The attacker deletes the real package from the registry
questions.explanation: Many build tools default to pulling whichever version number is highest across public and private registries. An attacker exploits this by publishing a public package with the same name and a higher version than the real internal one.

questions.q: What makes tool description poisoning dangerous for an agent?
options: It requires the attacker to gain direct code execution first
It only affects agents that use voice input
Hidden instructions inside a tool's description text are read by the agent as trusted instructions, with no code execution needed
It can only be performed by someone with database access
questions.explanation: The agent treats a tool's description as part of its own instructions. An attacker can hide commands directly in that text — no exploit or code execution required, just words the model reads and obeys.

questions.q: What is the single most important defense layer for securing AI agents?
options: Using the largest possible language model
Writing very detailed rules inside the system prompt
Least privilege — giving every tool and agent the minimum access it actually needs
Trusting tool outputs since they come from your own systems
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits the damage even if the model is fully manipulated — if a tool physically cannot reach data or actions beyond its scope, there's nothing an attacker can trick it into misusing.

questions.q: What is the purpose of requiring human approval for high-impact agent actions?
options: It makes the agent respond faster
It removes the need for any other security controls
It turns a potentially automatic, catastrophic action into just a request a person can reject
It is only useful for actions involving images
questions.explanation: Even if the agent is fully tricked into proposing a harmful action, a human-in-the-loop approval step means it still can't be completed without a person confirming it.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of sandboxing risky operations like code execution or document parsing?
options: It makes the agent's responses more creative
Even if an attacker escapes into the sandbox, there is nothing valuable to steal and nowhere further to go
It removes the need for logging
It speeds up every tool call
questions.explanation: A sandbox with no secrets, no meaningful network access, and disposable containers means a successful compromise still leads nowhere useful for the attacker.

questions.q: What is the 'golden rule' emphasized across the agent security defenses?
options: Enforce security in code and the orchestrator — never rely on the prompt alone
Always use the newest available model version
Trust the model's own judgment about what is safe
Keep the system prompt as short as possible
questions.explanation: A rule in the system prompt is only a suggestion a clever attacker can talk the model out of. A check enforced in actual code is a hard barrier the model cannot bypass no matter how it's manipulated.
